description: Core engine deep-dive: clock DST edge cases, RNG seed propagation, telemetry accumulation, domain solver ordering, zone temperature updates, diagnostics pipeline, autosizing oversizing factors and design temperature fallback, synthetic building RC validity, solver builder wiring, and dwelling conversions.

reviews.title: Clock DST transition edge cases: spring-forward 23h, fall-back 25h, leap day Feb-29
reviews.prompt: Daylight Saving Time transitions create two pathological edge cases for any scheduler: (a) spring-forward where 02:00-03:00 does not exist (23-hour day), and (b) fall-back where 01:00-02:00 occurs twice (25-hour day). For spring-forward, verify that the clock correctly skips the nonexistent hour and does not produce duplicate timesteps or index-in-range panics. For fall-back, verify that the ambiguous hour is resolved unambiguously—either by always using the first occurrence (standard time preference) or by using UTC offsets. A common bug is comparing wall-clock times across the DST boundary using naive datetime arithmetic, which produces off-by-one-hour errors for half the year. Also verify leap-day handling: Feb-29 must increment day-of-year counters correctly and not cause month-length assumptions to fail. Review the timestamp generation for all 365/366 days of a DST-observing year, checking that each timestep is exactly the configured simulation interval apart in UTC (wall-clock gaps are expected; UTC gaps are bugs). Check whether the clock accepts an IANA timezone string or only fixed UTC offsets—an offset-only clock cannot model DST transitions at all, making region-specific tariff alignment (TOU periods defined in local time) break during DST. If the clock does not handle DST, flag this as a prerequisite for any North American or European deployment.

reviews.title: RNG seed propagation: config to Dwelling to per-actor streams, checkpoint/restore determinism
reviews.prompt: Stochasticity in HARES covers occupancy, equipment cycling, weather variability, and control randomization. The RNG seed must flow from the top-level simulation config through each Dwelling to per-actor streams (thermal noise, occupant behavior, equipment state transitions) such that: (1) Each actor within a dwelling gets an independent, non-overlapping RNG stream. Splitting a single global RNG by incrementing a counter is fragile; verify the seeding strategy uses a cryptographically sound split (e.g., ChaCha with per-stream nonce) or a seedable RNG hierarchy (master seed → dwelling seed → actor seeds derived via hash). (2) In fleet mode with multiple dwellings, verify that dwellings do not share RNG state—a common bug is cloning the dwelling RNG before reseeding per-dwelling, causing identical random sequences for every dwelling. (3) Checkpoint/restore must preserve exact RNG state for deterministic replay. A checkpoint must serialize the full RNG internal state (not just the seed) so that restoring from checkpoint continues the exact same random sequence. Verify that RNG state is included in the checkpoint payload and restored before any step execution. (4) Test that re-running with the same config seed produces identical outputs (within floating-point tolerance). Any non-determinism in random number streams breaks scientific reproducibility and invalidates A/B comparisons.

reviews.title: Telemetry accumulation: CoreOutput and CoreState aggregation, fuel_type indexing consistency
reviews.prompt: All simulation output data flows through the telemetry layer. Review the CoreOutput and CoreState structs for completeness: every physical quantity computed during a step (zone temperatures, humidity, power draws, fuel consumption, energy storage levels, control signals, DV outputs) must have a corresponding field. Missing fields mean data is computed but unreportable. Check the accumulation logic: per-equipment PortContribution values are summed into CoreOutput; verify that the accumulation window (a single timestep vs. a billing period vs. simulation-total) is clearly defined and that partial-step contributions (e.g., a heat pump that cycles mid-step) are correctly prorated. The fuel_type field is used to index per-fuel accumulators—verify that the fuel_type enum is used consistently throughout the accumulation code (no magic strings, no off-by-one index errors). Check that all fuel types defined in FuelType have corresponding accumulator slots and that a newly added fuel type would fail to compile (or at least produce a visible error) rather than silently drop data. Finally, verify the telemetry reset behavior at the start of each timestep, period, or billing cycle—stale data from a previous period contaminating the current accumulation is a common source of subtle output errors.

reviews.title: Domain solver execution order: thermal→electrical→humidity→fluid, coupling errors
reviews.prompt: The domain solver execution order within the dwelling step creates implicit coupling assumptions that, if violated, produce physically wrong results. The prescribed order is: thermal first, then electrical, then humidity, then fluid last. Review each dependency: (a) Thermal before electrical: temperature-dependent loads (heat pump COP, battery efficiency, conductor resistance) need updated zone temps. If electrical runs before thermal, it uses stale temperatures. (b) Humidity after thermal: latent heat exchange (evaporation, condensation) depends on thermal conditions. Running humidity before thermal decouples latent and sensible loads, violating the psychrometric relationship. (c) Fluid last: DHW draw, hydronic loop flows, and water heater operation respond to electrical availability (for heat pump water heaters) and thermal conditions. Verify the actual execution order in dwelling/mod.rs matches this prescribed order. Check for any parallel solver execution that might violate ordering constraints. Also verify the environment-to-device feedback path: after each solver, does the dwelling update its internal state (zone temps, humidity, power draw) before the next solver reads it? If all solvers read from a snapshot taken at the start of the step, there is no cross-solver coupling within the step—flag this as a one-step-lag design with implications for coupled dynamics (e.g., a heat pump water heater should see the same-step electrical load to avoid overloading the panel). Compare against EnergyPlus's zone heat balance iteration approach.

reviews.title: Zone temperature update after thermal solver: flow to EnvironmentState before equipment step
reviews.prompt: After the thermal solver completes, updated zone temperatures must propagate to EnvironmentState before any equipment step executes. Equipment controllers read current zone temperature from EnvironmentState to make mode decisions (heat/cool/off) and to calculate runtime fraction. Stale zone temperatures cause equipment to heat when cooling is needed, or vice versa. Review the update path: thermal solver output → zone temperature array → EnvironmentState update → equipment step reads EnvironmentState. Check that (a) all conditioned zones are updated, including those with no active equipment (which still need accurate temperatures for thermostat deadband logic), (b) unconditioned zones (garage, attic, crawlspace) are also updated—these influence envelope heat transfer to conditioned zones, and (c) the update happens atomically: no equipment step reads a partially updated state. Also verify that the temperature array index mapping (zone ID to array position) is consistent across the thermal solver output, EnvironmentState, and equipment zone_id fields. A common bug is zone ID 0 (None/outdoor) leaking into the indoor zone array, causing an index panic or silently corrupting the first indoor zone temperature.

reviews.title: Diagnostics pipeline: NaN detection, negative energy, telemetry consistency, zero overhead in production
reviews.prompt: The diagnostics pipeline provides runtime correctness checks: NaN detection in all floating-point values, negative energy detection (total delivered energy should never be negative over a billing period), telemetry consistency checks (sum of per-equipment output equals dwelling total), and invariant checks. Review the implementation for performance impact: diagnostics must not add measurable overhead to production simulation runs. Check whether diagnostics are gated behind a feature flag, compilation cfg, or runtime toggle. If diagnostics are always compiled in but gated by a runtime flag, verify that the flag check is branch-predictable (cold path) and that the diagnostics data is not collected when disabled (not just not reported—collecting data and then discarding it still costs memory and CPU). For NaN detection: verify that the check covers all intermediate and output floating-point values, not just the final output. A NaN that originates in the humidity solver and propagates through five steps before surfacing is harder to debug than a NaN caught at origin. For negative energy: verify the check uses an appropriate tolerance (very small negative values from floating-point roundoff should not trigger false positives). Check that diagnostics messages include enough context (timestep, dwelling ID, zone, equipment ID) to trace the root cause without re-running with more logging.

reviews.title: Autosizing oversizing factors: 1.4x heating, 1.15x cooling, ACCA Manual S-2017 compliance
reviews.prompt: The autosizing module applies oversizing factors to design loads: 1.4x for heating, 1.15x for cooling. These factors must be verified against ACCA Manual S-2017 (Residential Equipment Selection). Manual S specifies maximum oversizing limits to prevent short-cycling: 1.4x for heating is generally acceptable (cold-climate furnaces may go higher), but 1.15x for cooling is aggressive—Manual S allows up to 1.3x for cooling in some climates. An undersized unit will fail to maintain setpoint on design days; an oversized cooling unit will short-cycle, provide poor dehumidification, and reduce efficiency. Review whether the oversizing factors should vary by: (a) climate zone (hot-dry climates can tolerate more cooling oversizing than hot-humid because latent load is lower), (b) equipment type (variable-speed heat pumps self-modulate and tolerate more oversizing than single-stage units; furnaces can be oversized more than heat pumps), and (c) building thermal mass (high-mass buildings can tolerate larger equipment because thermal lag buffers short-cycling). Check whether the autosizing code applies the factor to the design load or to the selected equipment capacity—these differ when equipment is available in discrete sizes and the code rounds up. Also verify that the oversizing factor is configurable (not hardcoded) for users who want to override the defaults.

reviews.title: Autosizing design temperature fallback chain: EPW header → ASHRAE 152 station → hardcoded defaults
reviews.prompt: The autosizing design temperature determination follows a fallback chain: (1) EPW file header design conditions, (2) ASHRAE 152 station data, (3) hardcoded defaults of -10°C heating and 35°C cooling. Review each fallback step for correctness and safety. Step 1 (EPW header): EPW files contain heating and cooling design temperatures with 99.6% and 0.4% annual cumulative frequency. Verify the parsing extracts the correct fields (not the extreme annual min/max or the monthly averages). Step 2 (ASHRAE 152 station): Verify that the station lookup matches the EPW location (latitude/longitude proximity or station WMO code). A mismatched station could provide design temps for a different climate zone. Step 3 (hardcoded defaults): -10°C/35°C are safe defaults for most US climates but are inappropriate for extreme climates (Fairbanks AK winter design temp is -43°C; Phoenix AZ summer design temp is 43°C+). The fallback must produce a safe (oversized) result, not a dangerous (undersized) result. Using -10°C for heating in Fairbanks would undersize by 33°C. Verify that the fallback is conservative—always errs on the side of overestimating the design load—and that if both EPW and ASHRAE data are missing, the code emits a strong warning rather than silently proceeding with potentially unsafe defaults. Also check whether the code distinguishes between the heating design temp (used for furnace sizing) and the cooling design temp (used for AC sizing)—applying the heating design temp to cooling calculations or vice versa would produce gross sizing errors.

reviews.title: Synthetic building RC network validity: physically plausible geometry, materials, specs
reviews.prompt: The synthetic building generator creates residential building models with physically plausible geometry, materials, and equipment specifications. These synthetic dwellings are used in every benchmark and many integration tests, so errors in synthetic generation propagate to all downstream validation. Review the RC network produced by the synthetic generator: (a) Geometry: wall areas, window areas, floor area, and volume must be mutually consistent (window-to-wall ratio physically plausible, ceiling height × floor area ≈ volume, surface areas sum to a closed envelope). (b) Materials: R-values, thermal mass (capacitance), and solar heat gain coefficients must be within physically plausible ranges. A wall with R-value 0 or infinite thermal mass will produce nonsensical dynamics. (c) Equipment sizing: equipment capacities should be proportional to floor area and climate zone (a 50 m² apartment does not need a 20 kW furnace). (d) Numerical stability: the resulting RC network must be numerically stable for the given timestep. Eigenvalues of the state-space matrix should have magnitudes < 1 for the discrete-time system. Unstable RC networks produce exponentially growing temperatures that crash the solver. Review how the generator handles edge cases like zero-area surfaces (removed rather than producing singular matrices) and extreme climate zones. Also verify that the generator is deterministic (given a seed, produces identical outputs) so that benchmarks are reproducible.

reviews.title: SolverBuilder wiring: boundary types, zone labels, surface properties, film coefficients
reviews.prompt: The SolverBuilder translates HPXML building descriptions into thermal solver inputs: boundary types (external, ground, adiabatic, interzone), zone labels (conditioned, unconditioned, garage, attic, crawlspace), surface properties (area, orientation, tilt, construction assembly), and film coefficients (interior and exterior convective resistance). Review each translation step for correctness: (a) Boundary type mapping: an HPXML surface attached to 'outside' must become an external boundary with the correct outdoor temperature node and combined convective/radiative film coefficient. A surface attached to 'ground' must use ground temperature boundary conditions (typically a deep-ground temperature or a ground-coupling model). Interzone surfaces (between two conditioned zones, or between conditioned and unconditioned) must connect to the correct pair of thermal nodes. (b) Zone labeling: verify that the HPXML zone IDs map correctly to solver zone indices and that all surfaces within a zone are aggregated into the correct thermal node. A surface accidentally assigned to the wrong zone creates phantom thermal coupling. (c) Film coefficients: each surface needs an interior film coefficient (typically 0.12 m²K/W for vertical surfaces, 0.16 for ceilings, 0.09 for floors per ASHRAE) and an exterior film coefficient (typically 0.03-0.04 m²K/W depending on wind speed). Verify that the solver builder assigns per-surface coefficients, not a single global coefficient. (d) Orientation and tilt: solar radiation calculations depend on correct surface azimuth and tilt. Verify these are passed through to the solar radiation model. (e) Missing or unrecognized HPXML elements: verify the builder fails with a clear error, not a silent default that produces plausible but wrong results.

reviews.title: Dwelling conversions: HPXML to equipment/config types, unit conversions, precision loss
reviews.prompt: The conversions module performs all type transformations from HPXML parsed data (string-based, unit-annotated) to Rust domain types (strongly typed, SI units). Every conversion must be correct and lossless. Review: (a) Unit conversions: HPXML uses a mix of SI and IP units (e.g., area in ft² or m², power in W or Btu/h, temperature in °F or °C, volume in gallons or liters). Verify that the unit parsing reads the HPXML unit annotation and applies the correct conversion factor. A missing unit annotation that defaults to the wrong system produces silent errors. (b) Numeric precision: intermediate conversions should use f64 (double precision) throughout. Accidental f32 truncation in a chain of conversions (e.g., Btu/h → W → kW) can drop 3-4 significant digits. (c) Type conversions: HPXML optional fields translate to Rust Option<T>. Verify that missing optional values produce None, not a default value (0.0, empty string) that has semantic meaning. (d) Enum mapping: HPXML string enumerations (e.g., heating system type, fuel type, water heater type) must map to the correct Rust enum variant. An unrecognized HPXML value should produce an error, not a default variant that runs the wrong equipment model. (e) Cross-reference consistency: when HPXML references the same entity in multiple places (e.g., a water heater's fuel type in both the water heating system element and the fuel type element), the conversions should verify consistency or document which source takes precedence. Compare against OCHRE's Dwelling.py to verify that HARES's interpretation of HPXML fields matches the reference implementation.
